sections.title: The Blessings over the Five Species of Grain
sections.html:
The Sages instituted special blessings for the five species of grain, which are: wheat, barley, spelt, rye and oats.

In general, the five species of grain are annual plants, and if so, seemingly their blessing ought to have been "Borei Peri Ha-adama" ("who creates the fruit of the ground"); however, because of their importance, since the main part of a person's food – bread and cooked dishes – is made from them, the Sages instituted a special blessing for them, in order to thank God, may He be blessed, in a detailed manner for our main sustenance. Over bread: "Ha-motzi leḥem min ha-aretz" ("who brings forth bread from the earth"), and over cakes and cooked grain dishes: "Borei minei mezonot" ("who creates various kinds of nourishment").

In greater detail, the five species of grain can be eaten in five states, and in each state their blessing changes. Let us enumerate the five states:

1) One who eats raw kernels of wheat or barley, since they have not yet been elevated to their choice state, recites "Borei Peri Ha-adama." As for the after-blessing, there is a doubt (as explained in section 13).

2) One who eats flour of ground grain, since he ate them in their very worst form, they have descended from their original stature, and he recites over them the simplest blessing: "Shehakol nihya bi-dvaro" ("by whose word all things came to be") (SA 208:5).

3) If one cooked the grain kernels, such as groats, bulgur and Quaker oats, or made from their flour kinds of cooked dishes such as noodles and ptitim (pasta flakes) or pashtidot (baked casseroles), since they have been elevated to the level of a cooked dish that sustains the heart, he recites "Borei minei mezonot." And after he has eaten a kezayit of them (about half a kebeitza), he recites Al Ha-miḥya, which is a Me'ein Shalosh blessing (a blessing that is an abridgement of the three blessings of Birkat Ha-mazon) (SA 208:2).

4) If one kneaded the flour, baked it and made bread from it, he recites "Ha-motzi leḥem min ha-aretz" at the beginning and Birkat Ha-mazon at the end (168:9).

5) There is one more kind which has an intermediate status, between a cooked grain dish and bread, and that is pat ha-ba'a be-kisnin. That is, kinds of baked goods such as cakes and crackers, which on the one hand are baked goods like bread, and on the other hand people are not accustomed to establish a meal (keviat se'uda) on them as on bread, but rather to eat them as dessert. The Sages determined that if one ate them in the way people eat between meals, for pleasure or to calm one's hunger, since he does not intend to be satiated as in a regular meal, his eating does not have the stature of eating bread, and therefore he should recite Mezonot before them and Al Ha-miḥya after them. But if he established a meal on them, their law is like that of bread, and he must wash his hands with a blessing before them, and recite Ha-motzi and Birkat Ha-mazon over them. All this is because they are baked goods; but if one establishes his meal on noodles and ptitim, since they are cooked dishes and not baked goods, he always recites Mezonot and Al Ha-miḥya over them.

sections.title: What Is Pat Ha-ba'a Be-kisnin?
sections.html:
Three explanations are mentioned in the words of the Rishonim for the kinds of pat ha-ba'a be-kisnin (whose laws were explained at the end of the previous section). 1) Kinds of filled baked goods, such as hamantaschen and strudel. They are called pat ha-ba'a be-kisnin because the dough is a pocket (kis) that is filled with sweet things such as poppy seeds, cocoa and nuts (Rabbeinu Ḥananel). 2) Kinds of baked goods to whose dough a flavor was added that creates a difference between them and bread, for example tortes or biscuits that have a sweet taste; or malawaḥ, to whose dough a lot of oil is added (Rambam). 3) Kinds of hard baked goods that a person crunches (koses) with his teeth, such as pretzels, crackers and matzot (Rav Hai Gaon).

In practice, we are accustomed to regard all three of these types as pat ha-ba'a be-kisnin, their common denominator being that on the one hand they are baked goods like bread, and on the other hand people usually eat them casually. Therefore, as long as one does not establish a meal on them, one recites Mezonot before them and Al Ha-miḥya after them, and when one establishes a meal on them, their law is like bread in every respect (SA 168:7).1

Sometimes a person intends to eat a little of a Mezonot baked good (pat ha-ba'a be-kisnin), and therefore he recites Mezonot at the beginning, but after he started eating he was drawn in and ate more and more until he ate the amount that constitutes establishing a meal; then, even though he recited Mezonot at the beginning, at the end he should recite Birkat Ha-mazon. And if, after tasting the Mezonot food, he decided to establish a meal on it, if what he intends to eat from now on contains the amount that constitutes establishing a meal, he should wash his hands and recite Ha-motzi. And if what he intends to eat afterwards does not contain the amount that constitutes establishing a meal, he may continue to eat on the basis of the Mezonot blessing he recited at the beginning. And at the end, since he ate the amount that constitutes establishing a meal, he should recite Birkat Ha-mazon (SA 168:6; MB 26).

sections.title: The Amount That Constitutes Establishing a Meal on a Mezonot Baked Good
sections.html:
As we have learned, a person who wishes to eat bread, even a very small amount, must recite Ha-motzi, because bread is meant for establishing a meal, and even if one eats only a little of it, one recites an important blessing over it. But over other baked goods made from the five species of grain, such as cakes and biscuits, since people are not accustomed to establish a meal on them, one recites Mezonot and Al Ha-miḥya. Only when one establishes a meal on them are they elevated to the level of bread, and then, in order to eat them, one must wash one's hands with a blessing, and recite Ha-motzi at the beginning and Birkat Ha-mazon at the end.

The amount that constitutes establishing a meal is the amount that people customarily eat at a regular meal, such that the diner leaves it satiated and does not need to eat again until the next meal. It is impossible to set a volume measure for this, because there are airy baked goods that satiate only when one eats a large amount of them, and there are dense baked goods that satiate with a relatively small amount. Rather, everything depends on what is customary: if people are accustomed to be satiated by what he intends to eat, he should recite Ha-motzi and Birkat Ha-mazon over it.

A person need not worry that perhaps he does not know what quantity people are accustomed to be satiated by, because whenever he eats an amount from which he is satiated in the way that he is satiated at a regular meal, he has established his meal on this eating, and he should recite Ha-motzi and Birkat Ha-mazon. Only one who knows that he is noticeably different from other people, for example that he becomes satiated from much less or much more, must estimate according to what is customary for most people. And even then he should estimate according to what seems right to him, and need not conduct in-depth research for this purpose.

Elderly people or children who become satiated with a smaller amount need not estimate according to most people, but according to what is customary among the elderly or children.

Some say that the amount that constitutes establishing a meal is a volume of four eggs (kebeitzot) of the Mezonot baked good, and even though people are not usually satiated by such an amount, people are already accustomed to establish a meal on this amount. In practice, we do not rule according to this view, and one who eats a volume of four eggs of the Mezonot baked good, as long as he did not eat the amount from which people are accustomed to be satiated at a regular meal, should recite Mezonot and Al Ha-miḥya. However, ideally (le-khatḥila), it is preferable not to eat an amount of four eggs, so as not to enter into a doubt. Rather, either he should eat less than a volume of four eggs, and then he recites Mezonot; or he should eat an amount from which people are accustomed to be satiated, and recite Ha-motzi and Birkat Ha-mazon according to all opinions.2

sections.title: Establishing a Meal When Eating Mezonot with Other Foods
sections.html:
One who intends to eat other foods together with the Mezonot baked good, such as salads and cheese, or meat and fish, should estimate everything together. If he eats from everything together an amount that satiates like a regular meal, the law of the Mezonot baked good is like that of bread. This is on condition that the Mezonot baked good is central to the meal, that is, that he eats of it at least a volume of four eggs. There is no difference whether the baked good is dense or airy – if it has a volume of four eggs, it is central to the meal. Only when the baked good has noticeable air pockets should one estimate the baked good without those pockets.

Thus there are two conditions here: 1) That he eats of the Mezonot baked good at least a volume of four eggs. 2) That he is satiated from everything he eats in the way people are accustomed to be satiated at a regular meal. If both conditions are fulfilled, he has established his meal on a Mezonot baked good, and he should wash his hands with a blessing and recite Ha-motzi over the baked good, and he should not recite blessings over the other foods, for they are exempted by the Ha-motzi blessing as in every meal. At the end of the meal he should recite Birkat Ha-mazon.

Just as a person need not worry that perhaps he does not know how to estimate the amount of satiety, so too a person need not worry that perhaps he is mistaken in estimating a volume of four eggs. For from the fact that this measure was given over to people without measuring instruments, it is implied that they knew that sometimes people would err upward and sometimes downward. Rather, everything depends on the judgment of the person eating, and whenever he estimates that the Mezonot baked good he is eating contains a volume of four eggs, and that together with the other foods he will be satiated, he is establishing his meal on the Mezonot baked good, and he must recite Ha-motzi and Birkat Ha-mazon without concern. (The measure of one egg is about 50 ml, and a regular cup of leben (yogurt drink) contains a volume of four eggs.)3

sections.title: How to Get Out of Situations of Doubt
sections.html:
Ideally, in order to get out of the doubt, it is proper to plan one's eating from the outset taking the two conditions into account: either one eats four eggs' worth of the Mezonot food and, together with the other foods, a satiating amount, and then according to all opinions he recites Ha-motzi and Birkat Ha-mazon. Or one eats less than a volume of four eggs of Mezonot and, together with the other foods, less than a satiating amount, and then according to all opinions he recites Mezonot and Al Ha-miḥya, and over the other foods he recites their own blessings.

If nevertheless he finds himself in doubt, in that he cannot decide whether what he intends to eat contains a satiating amount; or he knows that together with the other foods he is eating a satiating amount, but the amount of Mezonot is certainly less than a volume of four eggs – since he is in doubt, he should recite Mezonot and Al Ha-miḥya, and over the other foods he should likewise recite their own blessings. And it is better that he finish eating the Mezonot food before he eats a satiating amount, and recite Al Ha-miḥya over it, and thereby all the other foods he eats afterwards do not combine with the Mezonot baked good, and according to all opinions he recites Mezonot and Al Ha-miḥya over it, and over the other foods he recites their own blessings.

Here is the place to note a common mistake: sometimes people invite their relatives and friends to a party and wish to honor them with a satiating meal, but since they do not want to trouble them to wash their hands and recite Birkat Ha-mazon, instead of bread they bring crackers and cakes, and also serve them meat, fish, cold cuts, salads, pashtidot and compote. But according to halakha, since at such a meal people are accustomed to eat a volume of four eggs of the Mezonot baked good and also to be satiated, one must wash one's hands and recite Ha-motzi and Birkat Ha-mazon over the Mezonot baked good. And even when people do not eat a volume of four eggs, as we have learned, since they are satiated, they enter into a doubt. And sometimes sweet rolls are served there, and people think their blessing is Mezonot. They make two mistakes: 1) Generally these rolls are considered bread, and even one who eats a little of them must recite Ha-motzi (as explained in the next section). 2) Generally people eat more than a volume of four eggs of them. Therefore, one who wishes to give his guests a meal that will satiate them should properly prepare bread there, and thus everyone will know that they must wash their hands and recite Ha-motzi, and thereby they will all merit to recite at the end the long Birkat Ha-mazon, which is a Torah commandment and contains four important blessings.4

sections.title: Sweet Ḥalla
sections.html:
As we have learned, a Mezonot baked good (pat ha-ba'a be-kisnin) has an intermediate status: if one eats it between meals, one recites Mezonot and Al Ha-miḥya, and if one establishes a meal on it, one recites Ha-motzi and Birkat Ha-mazon. But over bread, even when one eats a little, one recites Ha-motzi and Birkat Ha-mazon. The question is where the boundary between bread and a Mezonot baked good lies.

The rule is that whatever people are accustomed to establish a meal on has the law of bread, whereas whatever people are accustomed to eat between meals, as a sweet or to somewhat calm one's hunger, has the law of a Mezonot baked good. Accordingly, the law of sweet ḥalla and sweet rolls is like bread, since people are accustomed to eat them at meals, and are not accustomed to serve them as a snack between meals. People are also accustomed to eat them with various salads, or to make a sandwich of them with cheese or tuna; thus they treat them as bread. Therefore, even when one eats a little of them, one must recite Ha-motzi and Birkat Ha-mazon over them. In our language, whatever is called bread or ḥalla or a roll – people are accustomed to establish a meal on it. In contrast, if a baked good is called "cake" or "cracker" and the like – people are not accustomed to establish a meal on it. Over a baked good about which there is a doubt whether it is bread or cake, one recites Mezonot. One who wishes to get out of the doubt should establish a meal on it and recite Ha-motzi (as explained above, sections 3-4), or eat it within a bread meal for the purpose of satiety, and then the Ha-motzi blessing he recites over the bread will exempt it according to all opinions.

Admittedly, many of Sephardic descent were accustomed to recite Mezonot over sweet ḥalla, because in the past people were not accustomed to serve it at a meal, but rather to serve slices of sweet ḥalla as refreshments between meals. However, in practice, since today ḥalla or a sweet roll is intended for meals and not as dessert between meals, one should always recite Ha-motzi and Birkat Ha-mazon over them.5

sections.title: Matza
sections.html:
When one establishes a meal on matza, it is clear that one recites Ha-motzi and Birkat Ha-mazon over it. The question is what the law is when one eats matza not within the framework of establishing a meal.

Some say that its blessing is Mezonot, because one of the definitions of pat ha-ba'a be-kisnin is a hard baked good that a person crunches with his teeth, such as crackers and matza crackers (matziyot). And since our matzot too are hard – their blessing is Mezonot. Admittedly, on Pesaḥ, when matza serves as bread, even one who eats a little of it recites Ha-motzi and Birkat Ha-mazon, but during the rest of the year one recites Mezonot over it (Ginat Veradim).

In contrast, many poskim wrote that since matza serves as bread on Pesaḥ, throughout the year its law is like bread. In addition, there is a difference between the purpose of matza and the purpose of crackers and matza crackers, for people are accustomed to establish a meal on matza, whereas matza crackers and crackers are eaten as dessert and as a snack. Therefore, even when one eats matza casually, one recites Ha-motzi and Birkat Ha-mazon over it. And this is the custom of those of Ashkenazic descent.

The custom of those of Sephardic descent is to take into account the opinion that throughout the year the law of matza is like that of crackers and matza crackers, whose blessing is Mezonot. Admittedly, ideally it is desirable to get out of the doubt and eat matza within a bread meal, exempting it with the Ha-motzi blessing. But one who wishes to eat matza not within the framework of a meal, according to the custom of those of Sephardic descent, should recite Mezonot (Yeḥaveh Da'at 3:12). And on the night after Pesaḥ and on Isru Ḥag of Pesaḥ, as long as people have not been able to buy bread, even according to the custom of those of Sephardic descent one should recite Ha-motzi over matza, because at that time matza is considered bread (Or Le-Tzion 12:3).6

sections.title: A Baked Good Filled with Cheese or Meat; Bourekas
sections.html:
A question has arisen regarding the law of baked goods whose dough is like bread dough, and which contain a filling of cheese or meat.

Some say that their blessing is Mezonot, for one of the definitions of the baked goods called pat ha-ba'a be-kisnin is that they are filled, and since a filling of cheese or meat was put inside the bread, people are not accustomed to establish a meal on it, and its blessing is Mezonot (Tanya; Taz 168:20).

And some say that only kinds of baked goods filled with sweet things, such as sugar and poppy seeds, are considered pat ha-ba'a be-kisnin, whose blessing is Mezonot. But if the filling is of the kinds of foods that people customarily eat together with bread, such as meat or cheese, people are accustomed to establish a meal on it, and the law of the baked good is like that of bread, and its blessing is Ha-motzi (Riaz; Shela; and so is implied by SA 168:17).

In practice, the law depends on the purpose of the baked good. If it is a baked good on which people are accustomed to establish a meal, its law is like bread, and even when one eats a little of it, one recites Ha-motzi and Birkat Ha-mazon. And if it is a baked good that people are accustomed to eat as a snack between meals, its blessing is Mezonot and Al Ha-miḥya, and only when one establishes a meal on it does one recite Ha-motzi and Birkat Ha-mazon. Generally, a large baked good is intended for establishing a meal, and a small one is intended as a snack. But over bourekas, even when it is large, as long as one did not establish a meal, one recites Mezonot, since its dough too is very different from bread, as oil is mixed into it.7

sections.title: Pizza
sections.html:
In the vast majority of cases the law of pizza is like that of bread, because pizza dough is like bread dough. And although yellow cheese, tomato paste and various spices are placed on the dough, they do not change the law of the base, which is bread. Thus the law of pizza is like that of a slice of bread on which various spreads have been spread, that even if one ate a little of it, one recites Ha-motzi and Birkat Ha-mazon over it.

But if it is a special pizza whose flour was kneaded with egg or milk, and as a result the taste of its baked dough is different, its law is like that of pat ha-ba'a be-kisnin, and when one does not establish a meal on it, its blessing is Mezonot and Al Ha-miḥya. And when one establishes a meal on it, its blessing is Ha-motzi and Birkat Ha-mazon. As we have learned (in sections 3-4), there are two conditions for establishing a meal: first, that one eats of the Mezonot baked good a volume of at least four eggs; and second, that one is satiated as is usual at a regular meal.8

sections.title: Over a Cooked Dish One Always Recites Mezonot
sections.html:
Everything we have learned, that sometimes one recites Ha-motzi over a Mezonot baked good, is because we are dealing with a baked good. But over cooked dishes of grain, such as noodles and ptitim, and likewise porridge made of grain, even if one eats a large quantity of them and establishes a meal on them – one always recites Mezonot and Al Ha-miḥya. The reason the Sages distinguished between baked goods and cooked dishes is that all kinds of baked goods resemble bread to a certain extent, both in their form and in their preparation by baking. Therefore, when one eats a Mezonot baked good between meals – one recites Mezonot and Al Ha-miḥya, and when one establishes a meal on it – one recites Ha-motzi and Birkat Ha-mazon. But cooked dishes are entirely different from bread, and therefore even when one establishes a meal on them, their blessing is Mezonot and Al Ha-miḥya.

The same law applies to Bissli and soup croutons (shkedei marak), for since they are made by deep-frying in oil, they are considered cooked, and even if one establishes a meal on them – their blessing is Mezonot and Al Ha-miḥya. The same law applies to sufganiyot (doughnuts): since they are cooked in deep oil – their law is like a cooked dish, and even if one establishes a meal on them their blessing is Mezonot and Al Ha-miḥya (and if they are baked sufganiyot, their law is like pat ha-ba'a be-kisnin).9

The same law applies to kugel: since the noodles are cooked first, even though the kugel is baked afterwards, since it did not take on the form of bread through the baking, and also beforehand the noodles were fit to eat, the law of the kugel remains that of a cooked dish, so that even if one establishes a meal on it – its blessing is Mezonot and Al Ha-miḥya.

sections.title: Various Baked Goods (Malawaḥ, Kubaneh, Blintzes, Pancakes, Waffles)
sections.html:
Malawaḥ is a kind of puff pastry, which is made in many layers, with margarine spread between one layer and the next. Afterwards the malawaḥ is fried in a pan with a little oil or baked in the oven. Since it contains a lot of margarine, even though it somewhat resembles a pita, its law is like pat ha-ba'a be-kisnin: if one establishes a meal on it, one recites Ha-motzi and Birkat Ha-mazon, and if one ate it casually between meals, one recites Mezonot and Al Ha-miḥya.

As we have learned, there are two rules in defining the establishing of a meal: first, that it contains a volume of four eggs, and second, that the diner is satiated, and it makes no difference whether the satiety comes from the Mezonot baked good alone or from the baked good together with other foods. One portion of malawaḥ contains close to a volume of four eggs, but people are not satiated by it as they are satiated at a regular meal. Therefore, one who intends to eat one portion should recite Mezonot and Al Ha-miḥya, and one who intends to eat two portions, or one portion with other foods, in the amount from which people are accustomed to be satiated at a regular meal, should wash his hands and recite Ha-motzi and Birkat Ha-mazon.

One who intends to eat slightly more than one portion – it is doubtful whether he will eat the amount that constitutes establishing a meal; therefore, one who knows that he will be satiated by it should recite Ha-motzi and Birkat Ha-mazon, and one who is in doubt should recite Mezonot and Al Ha-miḥya.

The same law applies to kubaneh and jaḥnun, which are dough-based baked goods baked inside a pot: since they contain a lot of oil, they are not considered bread, and therefore one who eats them between meals recites Mezonot and Al Ha-miḥya. And if he established a meal on them, he recites Ha-motzi and Birkat Ha-mazon. The same is the law of a tortilla: its blessing is Mezonot, and if one established a meal on it, its law is like bread.

There are foods made from a soft batter on a pan, such as pancakes, laḥoḥ, blintzes, Belgian waffles and French crêpes, and since their final form is like the form of a baked good, their law is like pat ha-ba'a be-kisnin: one who establishes a meal on them washes his hands with a blessing, and recites Ha-motzi and Birkat Ha-mazon.

One who is in doubt whether he will eat of one of these foods an amount from which people are satiated should recite Mezonot; and one who estimates that he will be satiated but is in doubt whether it is an amount from which most people are satiated should recite Ha-motzi and Birkat Ha-mazon (as explained at the end of note 2).10

sections.title: Fried Bread, Croutons, Fried Matzot
sections.html:
As is known, because of the importance of bread, the Sages established special blessings for it, Ha-motzi and Birkat Ha-mazon. The question is what one recites over kinds of bread that were cooked or fried: does one still recite Ha-motzi over them, or have they descended from their stature so that one recites Mezonot over them?

The rule is that if the pieces of bread that were cooked are larger than a kezayit (the volume of half an egg), even if their form changed and they do not look like bread, since they are larger than a kezayit, the law of bread remains upon them and their blessing is Ha-motzi. And if the pieces of bread that were cooked are smaller than a kezayit, even if the form of bread remained upon them, they have descended from their stature, and even if one establishes a meal on them, their blessing is Mezonot. Therefore, over croutons manufactured in factories one recites Mezonot, because they are pieces of bread smaller than a kezayit that were cooked in deep oil.

But one who prepares croutons from pieces of bread by baking them in the oven – even if they are smaller than a kezayit, since they did not undergo cooking and their form remained the form of bread – even over a single piece one recites Ha-motzi, and if one ate a kezayit of them one recites Birkat Ha-mazon at the end.

Breadcrumbs smaller than a kezayit that were consolidated and compressed or baked with other ingredients to create a cake or a patty – since they are smaller than a kezayit and do not have the form of bread – their blessing is Mezonot and Al Ha-miḥya.

One who fries slices of bread with egg – since the pieces are larger than a kezayit, according to all opinions he recites Ha-motzi and Birkat Ha-mazon over them. And if one fried pieces smaller than a kezayit and the form of bread remained upon them, there is a doubt about their blessing. For there is a doubt whether frying in a pan is considered cooking, in which case their blessing is Mezonot, or baking, in which case their blessing is Ha-motzi. In order to get out of the doubt, it is proper to eat them within a bread meal. And if one eats them by themselves, because of the doubt he should recite Mezonot.

Regarding fried pieces of matza (matza brei) too there is a doubt, since the form of matza remained upon them. Then, if frying is considered baking, their blessing is Ha-motzi and Birkat Ha-mazon; and if it is considered cooking, even if one establishes a meal on them, their blessing is Mezonot and Al Ha-miḥya. In order to get out of the doubt, it is proper first to eat a kezayit of bread or matza, recite Ha-motzi, and thereby also exempt the fried matza, and at the end to recite Birkat Ha-mazon. And one who does not wish to establish a meal on the fried matza, but only to taste some of it between meals, should recite Mezonot and Al Ha-miḥya over it.11

sections.title: Raw Grain Kernels, Shalva, Granola and Wheat Crackers
sections.html:
The usual way of eating the five species of grain is as a baked good or a cooked dish, and then their blessing is Ha-motzi or Mezonot. But one who eats kernels raw, or roasted, or slightly cooked, recites Ha-adama, for since he did not eat them in accordance with their stature, they are like other kinds of legumes, over which one recites Ha-adama.12

However, if an important food was prepared from them, such as wheat crackers (crispbreads), shalva (puffed wheat) and granola, since they are fully prepared, and people are accustomed to eat them as an important food that is not inferior to cooked grain dishes, their blessing is Mezonot and Al Ha-miḥya.13
